rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some commentators connect the verse to idolaters demanding a sign, including turning Ṣafā into gold or asking how one God can encompass all people.
rows.anchor: Some attach this verse to a specific challenge posed by the idolaters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly presents natural and cosmic phenomena as divine signs, sometimes singly and sometimes in a series.
rows.anchor: The listing of such natural phenomena and cosmic events as signs of God appears throughout the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variation of night and day is cited as a sign elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: the variation of the night and the day (3:190; 10:6; 23:80; 45:5)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creation of the heavens and earth is cited as a sign elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: the creation of the heavens and the earth (3:190; 30:22; 42:29)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also mentions ships sailing at sea in several other passages.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ships are the verse’s sole human-made items, yet depend closely on nature and remain fragile against the sea, making seafaring itself a reminder of God.
rows.anchor: Ships are significant in being the only human-made items in this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other passages depict people turning sincerely to God during sea storms and lapsing after danger passes.
rows.anchor: human beings are said to turn to God sincerely, only to lapse when the storm has passed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revival of the earth after its death is another Quranic sign repeated in several passages.
rows.anchor: The revival of the earth after its death also appears in 16:65; 29:63; 30:19; 35:9; 45:5; 57:17

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Winds are signs and blessings, and the word rīḥ is root-related to rūḥ, or spirit.
rows.anchor: the word rīḥ (“wind”) is related by root to rūḥ(“spirit”)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Clouds course between earth and sky under divine subjection, like other things described as subjected to God or made useful to people.
rows.anchor: The clouds are made to course between the earth and the sky and are subdued

rows.speaker: Many commentators
rows.claim: Before this verse, fasting resumed after sleep: people could eat after sunset until the ʿishāʾ prayer, then sleep began the next day’s fast.
rows.anchor: Many commentators report that before the revelation of this verse, Muslims would fast after sleeping

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some say Muslims abstained from sex throughout Ramadan, even at night, though the source for this account is unclear.
rows.anchor: Some maintain that the Muslim community would abstain from sexual activity for the whole of Ramadan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse alleviates the earlier fasting requirements.
rows.anchor: This verse is considered an alleviation of those requirements

rows.speaker: Commentators
rows.claim: Commentators report that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb admitted having intercourse with his wife after she said she had fallen asleep, then regretted it and sought recourse.
rows.anchor: It is reported that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, the prominent Companion and second Caliph, confessed to having had sexual relations

rows.speaker: Commentators
rows.claim: Commentators recount that Qays ibn Ṣirmah fell asleep before eating after a hard day’s fasting and therefore continued fasting the following day.
rows.anchor: Commentators also mention Qays ibn Ṣirmah, who came home after a harsh day of work while he was fasting

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK lists possible senses of seeking what God prescribed: seeking children, obeying Quranic commands, seeking the Night of Power, accepting ritual latitude, or lawful intercourse.
rows.anchor: or seek to have sexual relations in a legitimate way (IK)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The white thread and black thread signify dawn and night; Q explains the white thread as an idiom for daytime.
rows.anchor: The white thread and the black thread refer to dawn and the night, respectively; “the white thread” is an idiom for the day (Q)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Hadiths discuss the dawn light that ends the night, including signs in the sky and illumination on mountain tops.
rows.anchor: whether the indication is seeing light in the sky itself or the illumination of the tops of mountains (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iʿtikāf is retreat in a mosque for a period devoted to prayer and remembrance.
rows.anchor: Retreat in the mosques refers to the practice of iʿtikāf

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: Reports say the Prophet spent Ramadan’s final ten days in mosque retreat.
rows.anchor: the Prophet would spend the last ten days of Ramadan in the mosque in iʿtikāf

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: During his final Ramadan, the Prophet spent twenty days in retreat.
rows.anchor: during his final Ramadan he spent twenty

rows.speaker: Commentators
rows.claim: Commentators typically identify the man who passed the ruined town as Ezra.
rows.anchor: Commentators typically identify the man in this verse as Ezra

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Other identifications name Ezekiel or Khiḍr.
rows.anchor: but others mention Ezekiel and even Khiḍr

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Some interpret the figure as an ordinary disbeliever shown the reality of resurrection, rather than a saint or prophet.
rows.anchor: Others say that this verse refers not to a saint or prophet, but to a disbeliever who is shown the reality of Resurrection (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The town’s roofs had collapsed and its walls fallen on them; khāwiyah also suggests emptiness.
rows.anchor: Fallen upon its roofs means that the roofs had collapsed and the walls fell onto them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about how long he tarried recurs in the sleepers’ account and in a soul’s questioning on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: The question How long hast thou tarried? is also asked of the sleepers in the cave

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some say the donkey’s bones were revived and clothed with flesh.
rows.anchor: Some say that the bones of the donkey were made to come back to life and be clothed with flesh

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others take the bones being reassembled and clothed to refer to the man himself.
rows.anchor: others believe this phrase refers to the man himself (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Some infer that being made a sign means the man was made a prophet.
rows.anchor: It is thought by some that God’s making this person a sign means that he was made a prophet (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being a sign does not establish prophethood, since Pharaoh too was made a sign and was no prophet.
rows.anchor: elsewhere Pharaoh was also made a sign (10:92), and he is the opposite of a prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the man was a prophet, his question expresses a wish to see resurrection, like Abraham’s question in the next verse, rather than pernicious doubt.
rows.anchor: his question is not taken as one of pernicious doubt, but in the same spirit as the question posed by Abraham in v. 260

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that God multiplies reward echoes the Quranic promise to reward the best deeds and increase from divine bounty.
rows.anchor: And God multiplies for whomsoever He will is echoed in 24:38

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wāsiʿ, the All-Encompassing, also means generous.
rows.anchor: al-Wāsiʿ) also means “generous.” The

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A prophetic report says good deeds may be multiplied tenfold or seven hundredfold, while fasting is reserved for God’s own reward.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is reported to have said, “God makes the good deed of the son of Adam to be tenfold, or seven hundred fold

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A man who offered a camel in God’s way was told he would receive seven hundred camels on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: a man came to the Prophet and said, “This camel I give in the way of God,” and the Prophet replied

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pride in generosity or reminding recipients of their need destroys charitable giving’s merit; a decent word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm.
rows.anchor: Exulting in one’s generosity or reminding the needy of their neediness destroys the virtue in charitable giving

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R says one should speak kindly to poor people and forgive harm they may cause through rough manner or embarrassment.
rows.anchor: It is better to offer an honorable word to the poor who ask for help and forgiveness for any harm they may cause

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R says to forgive the poor if their requests cause trouble or discomfort.
rows.anchor: if their asking causes one trouble or discomfort, one should forgive them for it (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving only to be seen is the worst model of charity, as also described in the Quran’s passage about ostentatious worshippers.
rows.anchor: The worst model of charity is one who gives only for appearance’s sake, as in 107:6–7

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain imagery contrasts charity spoiled by bad intention with giving done for God’s pleasure and secure faith.
rows.anchor: These verses compare the merit of two kinds of giving through the symbolism of rain striking the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain washes dust from a smooth rock and leaves no fertile benefit, illustrating giving without sincere intention.
rows.anchor: When a downpour strikes the earth on a smooth stone, it can only wash it away

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain on a fertile garden doubles its yield, symbolizing charity given with the right intention.
rows.anchor: the garden to double its yield, symbolizing the fruit of charity with the right intention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even without a downpour, a softer rain lets the garden thrive and bear fruit.
rows.anchor: even if the amount of rain is not great, the garden will at least thrive normally and bear its fruit

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators say elevated oases gather rich earth and flourish; because streams do not reach them, rain alone nourishes them.
rows.anchor: Some commentators mention that certain kinds of oases flourish and have rich earth collect on them when they are slightly elevated

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others read bi-rabwah as something that rises, meaning fertile soil from which crops grow upward.
rows.anchor: Others say that upon a hill (

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī argues hills lack streams and face too much wind, while hollows flood; he says level ground is best and prefers a meaning tied to growth.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī argues that a garden upon a hill would not be reached by streams and would be exposed to too much wind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says God grows a lawfully earned date given in charity until it becomes mountain-sized or larger.
rows.anchor: When a person gives a lawfully earned date in charity, God takes it in His Hand and causes it to grow

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: IK and Ṭ understand giving out of inner confirmation as expressing certainty of faith in the act of giving.
rows.anchor: means that the givers affirm and have certainty of faith in their act of giving (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Z reads inner confirmation as confirmation of God’s Truth or certainty.
rows.anchor: that they do so because they have confirmation of the Truth of God or certainty (Z)

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Q and R understand the phrase as giving carefully and confirming that charity is placed where it will be used properly.
rows.anchor: they take care and confirm where they place their charity to make sure that it is used properly (Q, R)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R reads the garden as charity’s fruit and the fiery whirlwind as later boasting and insults that destroy it, leaving the giver with nothing for the Hereafter or weak descendants to support him.
rows.anchor: For some this verse is a parable of those who follow up their charitable giving with preening and injury

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the verse as people doing good works and later evil works that wipe out the earlier deeds’ value.
rows.anchor: According to another interpretation attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, this verse refers to those who do good works

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every kind of fruit may mean many kinds of fruit.
rows.anchor: Every kind of fruit can mean something like “many kinds of fruit.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rivers running below is a common image for Paradise.
rows.anchor: With rivers running below is a common image symbolizing the paradisal state

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to give from good things echoes the Quranic statement that piety requires spending from what one loves.
rows.anchor: A similar message appears in 3:92: You will never attain piety till you spend from that which you love

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A famous hadith says belief is incomplete until one wants for a neighbor, or in another version a brother, what one wants for oneself.
rows.anchor: In a famous ḥadīth the Prophet stated, “None of you believes until he desires for his neighbor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good things may mean wholesome and desirable items one would not reject, or things that are lawful.
rows.anchor: Here good things can mean either what one considers wholesome and desirable, what one would not reject, or what is lawful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Charity should not be funded with unlawful or distasteful things.
rows.anchor: One should not seek unlawful or distasteful means to give in charity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Companions hung good dates in the mosque for the poor; another group brought inferior dates, and the verse was said to have been revealed then.
rows.anchor: It is reported that a group of Companions would bring bunches of dates from their date palms and hang them in the mosque

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says God apportions worldly provision to people regardless of His love, but grants religion only to those He loves.
rows.anchor: Truly God distributes your provisions among you, just as He distributes your virtues among you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same hadith says true submission requires heart and tongue submission and believers’ body parts being safe from lies and wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: no servant submits until his heart and tongue submit, and no believer believes until his bodily parts are safe from his misfortunes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hadith says charity from unlawfully earned wealth is not accepted, wrongdoing is erased by good rather than more wrongdoing, and one should not feed others what one would not eat.
rows.anchor: No servant receives blessing by earning wealth that is unlawful and giving it in charity

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK explains that Satan frightens people with poverty to stop charity and prompts other sins, while God recalls forgiveness and generosity to the soul.
rows.anchor: Satan makes one dread poverty, causing one to refrain from giving charity, and moreover inspires one to commit other sins and acts of disobedience, whereas God causes the soul to remember forgiveness and generosity (IK)

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says reluctance to give the best can begin with giving only leftovers, then grow into fear of giving any charity.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī argues, for example, that ideally people should give from the best that they have

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī traces miserliness through attachment to all desired things, passive obedience to Satan, abandoning good works, and committing evil.
rows.anchor: This miserliness then infects the rest of the soul, which struggles to keep all that it desires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith contrasts Satan’s inspiration to promise evil and lie against truth with an angel’s inspiration to urge good and affirm truth, advising praise of God or refuge from Satan accordingly.
rows.anchor: As for Satan’s inspiration, it is a promise to do evil and tell lies against the truth

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R says Al-Wāsiʿ can mean abundantly generous in forgiveness.
rows.anchor: Generous in His Forgiveness” (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Madinan surah’s title Āl ʿImrān means the House of ʿImrān, the family line named in verse 33.
rows.anchor: Madinan period, Āl ʿImrān, or “The House ofʿImrān,” refers to the family line

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Early discussion of Quranic interpretation raises the text’s levels of meaning and the spiritual qualities needed to understand it deeply.
rows.anchor: there is a discussion of the interpretation of the Quran (v. 7), raising questions of its levels of meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah recounts Mary’s birth and early life, Jesus’s birth and miracles, and his relationship with the apostles.
rows.anchor: the birth and early life of Mary, the mother of Jesus (vv.35–43), the birth of Jesus (vv. 45–47)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah strongly criticizes Jews and Christians among the People of the Book while distinguishing good from bad and affirming some as believers and upright.
rows.anchor: criticizing them strongly, but also distinguishing between the good and the bad among them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A substantial section addresses the Battle of Uḥud, fought by the believers against the Meccans in 3/625 outside Medina after Badr.
rows.anchor: A considerable portion of this sūrah is devoted to the events of the Battle of Uḥud (3/625)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Uhud section addresses cowardice, hypocrisy, worldly attachment, and theological questions including the soul’s state after worldly life.
rows.anchor: This part of the sūrah also deals, among other matters, with the moral issues of cowardice, hypocrisy, and worldly attachment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some traditions place the revelation of the surah’s first thirty to eighty verses during a visit to Medina by Christians from Najrān.
rows.anchor: It is said that the first part of this chapter (between thirty to eighty verses according to various opinions) was revealed on the occasion

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One Najrān delegate was said to have been honored by the Byzantines for religious knowledge.
rows.anchor: one of whom was said to be honored by the Byzantines for his knowledge of religion (R)

rows.speaker: Christians
rows.claim: In the traditional debate, Christians argued Jesus was God because he revived the dead, healed lepers, and spoke of unseen matters.
rows.anchor: they said that Jesus was God, because he revived the dead, healed lepers, and spoke of unseen realities

rows.speaker: Christians
rows.claim: They also called Jesus God’s son because he had no human father, and one of three because scripture uses divine first-person plural speech.
rows.anchor: that he was the son of God, because he had no human father; and that he was the third of three

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet challenged the sonship claim by asking whether children resemble their fathers and whether Jesus, unlike the living Lord, was subject to death; the Christians agreed.
rows.anchor: Do you not know that our Lord is Living and does not die, and that Jesus is subject to passing away

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet asked whether Jesus could sustain, preserve, guard, and provide for all things as God does; the Christians answered no.
rows.anchor: Do you not know that our Lord sustains all things, preserving them, guarding them, providing for them

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet argued that nothing is hidden from God and Jesus knew only what he had been taught; the Christians agreed.
rows.anchor: Do you not know that nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from God most high

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet contrasted God’s freedom from bodily needs with Jesus’s human birth, feeding, eating, drinking, and bodily functions, asking how the Christian claims could stand.
rows.anchor: God formed Jesus in the womb as He willed, and that our Lord does not eat food, nor consume drink

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account says the first part of the surah was revealed after the debate with the Christians.
rows.anchor: According to the account, it was after this that the first part of the chapter was revealed (Al, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āl ʿImrān follows al-Baqarah and is paired with it in virtue reports as the two radiant surahs, al-zahrāwiyān.
rows.anchor: Āl ʿImrān follows al-Baqarah, and in some of the aḥādīth describing the various “virtues” of the Quran it is paired with al-Baqarah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says Quran recitation intercedes for its devotees and the two radiant surahs appear on Judgment Day as clouds, sunrays, or flocks of birds pleading for them.
rows.anchor: Recite the Quran, and it will intercede on the Day of Resurrection for those who are devoted to it
